newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-FOREMAN BEATS SAVARESE IN SPLIT DECISION.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-FOREMAN BEATS SAVARESE IN SPLIT DECISION.

text.p: George Foreman, 48, traded punches toe-to-toe for 12 rounds with a very tough 31-year-old Lou Savarese to earn a split decision on Saturday.

There were no knockdowns in the fight, but Savarese took cuts over his left eye and on his right cheek. Savarese also had a point deducted by referee Eddie Cotton in the 11th round for low blows after several warnings.

Savarese was the 6-5 favourite in a fight that was much more entertaining than anticipated between the lumbering Foreman and the relatively inexperienced Savarese, who has faced few formidable opponents in his career.
The two big men at times seemed glued to each other as they leaned forward trying to untangle the other's arms and land short punches to the head.

Judge Barbara Perez scored the fight, before about 7,000 fans in the West Hall of the Atlantic City Convention Centre, 115-112 for Foreman. Al DeVito had it 114-113 for Savarese, and Safeeq Rashada had Foreman ahead 118-110.

Foreman, who had been respectfully cautious throughout most of the fight, was leaping in -- or as much as the rotund Foreman could leap -- with round-house punches in the 12th round in a bid to knock out Savarese.

Foreman, who won two heavyweight titles in 1994 with a 10th round knockout of Michael Moorer but was stripped of his crowns for ducking mandatory opponents, landed a huge left cross to Savarese's head in the early part of the round and followed with a left and a right.
But the tough Savarese would not go down. Foreman stumbled into the ropes after missing a right hand, but Savarese was not quick enough to hit him.
The eighth round was perhaps the best of the fight as both big men -- Foreman at 253 pounds (114.7 kg) and Savarese (230 pounds, 104.3 kg) -- whaled away at each other, both landing hard blows.

Foreman, who seemed to establish himself as a viable opponent for either Mike Tyson or Evander Holyfield, came out in the ninth round swaying rhythmically from side to side and giving a hint of dancing on his toes.
But Savarase brought Foreman to his flat feet with a left-right combination and Foreman soon resumed his plodding advance as he had throughout the fight.

Savarese fought Foreman's fight by standing in front of the still-powerful former two-time champion. But Foreman, who makes lumbering seem fast, was unable to extend his arms often to get the full force of his weight behind his punches, and was too slow to spin Savarese to get better angles.

Savarese came into the fight with a 36-0 record but only four of his first 30 victories were against opponents with winning records. Perhaps if he had fought better opponents he would have had the expertise to better deal with Foreman.

The fight was for something dubbed the "Linear Heavyweight Championship of the World" -- a figment of the promoters' imagination announced just moments before the fight. It had been billed for the lightly-regarded World Boxing Union title, but there was an apparent dispute over sanctioning fees and the WBU withheld its sanction, not that anyone really cared.
"It was a decision for me," said Foreman, now 76-4. "That's really all I care about. I did not understand how he stayed up with the shots I was giving him. I don't know where he got the strength.
"In the second half of the fight," said Foreman, who received about $4 million to Saverese's $500,000, "I was throwing more punches with a lot of power. He hurt me one time with an overhand right."

Savarese said: "I fought my best. George is a crafty guy. He hit me in the first round, and I couldn't see after that. I can take a punch. Whenever he hit me with one punch, I tried to come back with two and three."
Savarese, who went to the hospital after the bout to take stitches for his cuts, was asked why he was getting hit late in fight and said, "because I couldn't see the punches coming.
"I should have stayed in my own rhythm. I got caught up with mano-a-mano. If I could have seen better, I would have boxed more."
Foreman's promoter, Irving Azoff, said Foreman would fight again in August or September in his hometown of Houston.
